\section{Extended Experimental Specifications and Protocols}
\label{app:experimental_protocol}

Section~\ref{sec:experiments} gives the environment progression and main protocol. Tiger, Diagnosis, Bandit, and Tileworld have a fixed hidden state and a terminal commit. RockSample and Inspection interleave observation, navigation, and exploitation under Proposition~\ref{prop:factored}.

The core environments, Tiger, Diagnosis, and Bandit, use $1{,}000$ episodes per seed over $\{42,123,456,789,1024\}$ and support the SARSOP comparison. Tileworld and Inspection use $500$ per seed, with RockSample counts in its captions. Other batteries state their own episode counts and seeding rules, so estimates are not interchangeable: Tiger EFE uses $4.20$ observations in Table~\ref{tab:main} and $4.32$ in Table~\ref{tab:sarsop}. Cross-battery comparisons are identified explicitly, including Table~\ref{tab:budget_frontier}'s committed-reference column.

Means aggregate episodes across seeds. Primary tests use per-seed Welch comparisons and Holm--Bonferroni correction (Appendix~\ref{app:stats}), with core bootstrap intervals archived in \texttt{results\_\allowbreak bootstrap\_\allowbreak ci.csv}. Appendix~\ref{app:pomcp} varies POMCP's computational budget from $500$ to $5{,}000$ simulations per decision, distinct from sensing budget $B$. Specifications are in Appendix~\ref{app:envs}. All simulated environments use the Gymnasium Python interface \citep{towers2024}.

\paragraph{Tiger} \citep{kaelbling1998}. A tiger is hidden behind one of two doors. Listening identifies its door with probability $0.85$ at cost $1$. Opening a door commits and ends the episode, paying $+10$ if correct and $-100$ otherwise. The only sensing choice is whether to listen again.

\paragraph{Sequential diagnosis.} Diagnosis has one of $N{=}4$ hidden conditions. Its $K{=}2$ binary tests, each with accuracy $0.80$ and cost $1$, query different partitions that together distinguish all conditions. Naming the condition ends the episode, paying $+10$ if correct and $-50$ otherwise.

\paragraph{Structured bandit.} Bandit has one hidden variable identifying the best of $K{=}4$ arms, so evidence about one arm also bears on the others. Inspecting an arm gives a noisy yes/no signal of whether it is best (accuracy $0.80$, cost $0.5$). A terminal pull pays $+10$ for the best arm and $+1$ otherwise.

\paragraph{Tileworld.} A single target occupies an $N{\times}N$ grid ($N{=}6$, $|S|{=}36$). Each scan queries one binary digit of its row or column index (accuracy $0.80$, cost $1$). Three row bits and three column bits give six complementary partitions that jointly identify the cell. A terminal collect action declares a cell, paying $+10$ if correct and $-50$ otherwise. Figure~\ref{fig:tw_comparison} shows belief evolution.

\paragraph{RockSample} \citep{smith2004}. RockSample is the first environment in the suite where sensing is interleaved with movement. An $N{\times}N$ grid holds $K$ rocks at known positions, each with a hidden binary quality (good or bad), and the agent's own position is fully observable. Move actions change the agent's position. Check actions produce noisy observations of a chosen rock's quality, with an accuracy that decays with the agent's distance from that rock. Sampling collects the rock at the current position (good $+10$, bad $-10$). Exiting ends the episode from wherever the agent stands and gives $+10$. All actions cost $-0.5$. We evaluate four instances, written RS[$N$,$K$] for an $N{\times}N$ grid with $K$ rocks, namely RS[5,3], RS[7,4], RS[7,8], and RS[11,11]. Unlike the above environments, RockSample has interleaved observe-act dynamics with state transitions, the setting addressed by Proposition~\ref{prop:factored}.

Our cost-modified RockSample differs from \citet{smith2004} in six respects. Every action costs $0.5$, whereas the original charges neither moves nor checks. Rock positions are fixed but use our maps. Returns are undiscounted, with the $N^2+10K$ episode cap of Appendix~\ref{app:envs}, rather than limited by discounting. Exit pays from any cell instead of only the east edge, providing the unconditional $+9.50$ outside option relevant to POMCP's mean-backup analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:rocksample}).

Hidden rock qualities remain fixed after sampling, whereas the original turns a sampled good rock bad. Observable sample history identifies collected rocks, whose re-sampling gives zero sampling reward while still costing $0.5$. This preserves the hidden state required by Proposition~\ref{prop:factored}.

Finally, the sensor starts at accuracy $0.95$ and halves that accuracy every four cells of Euclidean distance, floored at $0.5$ (\texttt{rho\_\allowbreak aif/\allowbreak environments/\allowbreak rocksample.py}). It becomes exactly uninformative beyond approximately $3.7$ cells. The original starts at perfect accuracy and approaches chance asymptotically as sensor efficiency decays, never reaching it at finite range.

Charging checks under undiscounted returns makes sensing usage interpretable as a budget, but these modifications preclude comparison of absolute returns with published RockSample results. Our state counts include only the $2^K$ hidden quality vectors, excluding observable position, so RS[11,11]'s $|S|{=}2{,}048$ follows a different convention from larger literature counts.

\paragraph{Structural inspection.} In Structural Inspection, $N$ components sit at known spatial locations on a grid, and each has a hidden binary state (nominal/faulty, prior $p_{\text{fault}}{=}0.3$) that the agent is tasked with declaring. There are $K{=}2$ non-destructive test types, visual (accuracy $0.70$, cost $-0.5$) and detailed (accuracy $0.90$, cost $-2$). The agent navigates between components, runs tests, and declares a diagnosis for one component at a time, in whatever order its own navigation takes it, so a completed episode carries one declaration per component rather than a single terminal commit. An episode ends once every component has been declared, or earlier at a step cap. A correct nominal declaration pays $+2$, a correct fault declaration pays $+5$, a missed fault costs $-50$, a false alarm costs $-5$, and each move costs $-0.5$. Neither tests nor moves change fault states, so this is a factored observation POMDP. The environment maps directly to industrial inspection, medical screening, and fault detection domains. We evaluate $N{=}8$ ($|S|{=}256$) and $N{=}16$ ($|S|{=}65{,}536$).

\subsection{A Near-Optimal Constrained-POMDP Reference}
\label{app:cpomdp_details}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Estimated cap-constrained reference at EFE usage $B_{\mathrm{EFE}}$. $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ maximizes reward over mixtures of sampled SARSOP-Lagrangian policies with usage at most that budget. Gap is $R_{\mathrm{ref}}-R_{\mathrm{EFE}}$, and Gap \% is $100(R_{\mathrm{ref}}-R_{\mathrm{EFE}})/|R_{\mathrm{ref}}|$. Neither is a certified optimality gap. On each environment the best sampled reference is already feasible, so the cap does not bind. Values use five seeds and $300$ episodes per seed. The actually evaluated usage-matched Planning+IG grid weights produce the same rewards as EFE in this run.}
\label{tab:cpomdp}
%% Numbers in this table are produced by experiments/run_cpomdp_baseline.py
\tablefontsize
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Environment & $B_{\mathrm{EFE}}$ & $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ & $R_{\mathrm{EFE}}$ & Gap & Gap \% \\
\midrule
Tiger & $4.32$ & $5.016$ & $5.016$ & $0.000$ & $0.00\%$ \\
Diagnosis & $9.82$ & $-1.265$ & $-1.224$ & $-0.041$ & $-3.27\%$ \\
Bandit & $5.10$ & $6.314$ & $6.320$ & $-0.005$ & $-0.08\%$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Section~\ref{sec:sarsop} compared the family against a reference free to spend whatever sensing it likes. The budgeted framing of Section~\ref{sec:budget} calls for a second reference that is near-optimal subject to a charge on sensing. A constrained POMDP is a POMDP solved for the best reward attainable under a bound on an expected cost, here sensing usage. For the three environments of Section~\ref{sec:sarsop}, we extend the same SARSOP export with a literal per-unit usage penalty, which adds $\lambda \ge 0$ to each observation action's own cost $\text{cost}_j$, so its reward becomes $-(\text{cost}_j + \lambda)$. Solving to SARSOP's precision ($10^{-3}$) then gives, for that $\lambda$, a near-optimal solution to $\max_\pi \mathbb{E}_\pi[R] - \lambda\,\mathbb{E}_\pi[U]$ over the full space of POMDP policies (not the additive Planning+IG family). This penalized problem is the literal Lagrangian of the budgeted problem~\eqref{eq:budgeted} (Section~\ref{sec:budget_theory}), the relaxation that penalizes usage rather than rewarding information. An exact maximizer at rate $\lambda$ cannot be beaten in reward by any policy that spends no more sensing than it does, by the mirror image of the two-line argument Section~\ref{sec:budget_theory} gives for the information floor, so it is optimal under a cap set at its own usage. Sweeping $\lambda$ therefore collects constrained references across a range of budgets. The reference is near-optimal rather than certified exact, because SARSOP is a point-based approximate solver and the reported reward and usage are Monte Carlo estimates from simulated episodes.

Two definitions clarify what a penalty sweep can and cannot certify. The achievable region is the set of pairs of expected usage and expected reward that some POMDP policy attains, and its frontier is the curve giving the best reward attainable at each usage level. Strong Lagrangian duality holds for a finite discounted constrained MDP \citep{altman1999}, but the belief MDP here (the Markov decision process over beliefs that the POMDP is equivalent to) has a continuous state space, so we do not assume a zero duality gap carries over. Under strong duality every budget's constrained optimum would be attained by the penalized problem at some $\lambda$, so a fine enough sweep would recover the whole frontier. Under a duality gap some budgets have a constrained optimum that no $\lambda$ picks out, and the sweep misses those points. Either way, the swept points are supported points of the achievable region, points that a linear trade-off between reward and usage picks out, each attained by an actually solved policy. They therefore estimate the frontier from below, each up to the sampling error of its own reward and usage rather than as a certified population bound, so any duality gap makes the reference conservative about frontier achievability. For an optimality comparison the effect is the opposite. A reference that undershoots the constrained optimum makes our agents look closer to optimal than they are, so the measured gap to the reference is a lower bound on the true gap.

With the caveat stated, the protocol is a grid sweep over the penalty. Sweeping $\lambda$ over a log-spaced $12$-point grid ($\lambda \in [0, 100]$, $\gamma{=}0.999$, $5$ seeds $\times$ $300$ episodes per $\lambda$) traces an estimated upper concave envelope of the achievable $(\mathbb{E}[U], \mathbb{E}[R])$ region, the frontier of the previous paragraph once mixtures of policies are allowed, sampled at these 12 supported points rather than continuously. A per-episode mixture of two adjacent swept policies approximates any intermediate budget, the same mixture argument used for the Planning+IG shadow price (Definition~\ref{def:pi3}), though the approximation inherits whatever slack the constituent near-optimal solutions carry. $\lambda{=}0$ recovers the ordinary reward-only SARSOP solve of Table~\ref{tab:sarsop} as a sanity check.

The usage-matched Planning+IG grid weights evaluated in Table~\ref{tab:cpomdp} are $0.00$, $0.45$, and $1.07$ for Tiger, Diagnosis, and Bandit. They are nearest grid points selected on a lighter usage curve rather than crossing brackets. Each lies on a run of consecutive sampled weights with constant usage that also straddles $w{=}1$, namely $[0,19.3]$, $[0.316,19.3]$, and $[0.72,1.64]$ respectively in \texttt{results\_\allowbreak price\_\allowbreak usage\_\allowbreak curves.csv}. The corresponding rewards in \texttt{results\_\allowbreak cpomdp\_\allowbreak baseline.csv}, columns \texttt{R\_PIG} and \texttt{R\_EFE}, agree to the precision stored. This observed agreement is not a consequence of Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence} at weights other than $1$.

Table~\ref{tab:cpomdp} reports the comparison. The reference at $B_{\mathrm{EFE}}$ is the estimated feasible envelope of the sampled reference policies, the best reward attainable by a per-episode mixture of sampled policies whose expected usage is at most $B_{\mathrm{EFE}}$ (\texttt{rho\_\allowbreak aif/\allowbreak budget.py}, \texttt{feasible\_\allowbreak envelope}, shared with Section~\ref{sec:budget_frontier}). On all three environments the envelope selects a single sampled policy, the $\lambda{=}0$ policy on Tiger and Bandit and the $\lambda{=}0.05$ policy on Diagnosis. Its usage equals $B_{\mathrm{EFE}}$ on Tiger and lies below it on Bandit and Diagnosis, where $B_{\mathrm{EFE}}$ exceeds every sampled usage, so the usage cap does not bind. The estimated gap is zero on Tiger and $-0.08\%$ on Bandit, smaller in magnitude than the reward change between adjacent swept points, and $-3.27\%$ on Diagnosis, where the reference value is slightly below $R_{\mathrm{EFE}}$. The population constrained optimum is at least the expected reward of any feasible policy, so a negative estimated gap can reflect sampling error on either side or approximation error in the reference rather than a violation of that bound. $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{EFE}}$ are $1{,}500$-episode Monte Carlo estimates with standard errors ($\pm 0.12$--$0.39$) several times the gap, and the best feasible sampled Diagnosis policy uses $9.785$ observations against EFE's $9.824$, so a finer $\lambda$ grid near $0$ and more episodes per point would sharpen the estimate.

The SARSOP comparison concerns reward when sensing is unconstrained, while this reference compares rewards at the sensing level EFE actually uses, where EFE's measured reward, and that of the usage-matched Planning+IG weights, is empirically close to the estimated best (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak cpomdp\_\allowbreak baseline.csv}, \texttt{results\_\allowbreak cpomdp\_\allowbreak frontier.csv}, \texttt{experiments/\allowbreak run\_\allowbreak cpomdp\_\allowbreak baseline.py}). The reference does not extend to RockSample or Structural Inspection, where SARSOP is no longer a practical solver at the sizes we study (Section~\ref{sec:budget_positioning} and Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}), so an optimality-gap estimate there remains future work.

\subsection{Distractor Robustness under Reward-Irrelevant Sensing}
\label{app:distractor_details}

This subsection gives the full distractor study behind Section~\ref{sec:distractor}. A sensing budget fixes how much sensing is bought and leaves open what that sensing is about. \texttt{DistractorDiagnosisEnv} is an $8$-joint-state Diagnosis variant whose hidden state pairs a condition (the variable the commit action must identify, as in Diagnosis) with an independent binary nuisance bit. Commit rewards depend only on the $4$-way condition, and one added test, the distractor test, is informative only about the nuisance bit. Every observation model in the environment factors through exactly one of the two independent components, so the distractor test carries exactly zero information about the condition marginal (the agent's belief over the condition alone), a property that Appendix~\ref{app:distractor} states and verifies by unit test.

Planning+IG is swept over a sixteen-point log weight grid ($5$ seeds $\times$ $100$ episodes) with extra points inserted inside the one coarse step on which distractor spending first appears, so the onset, the first weight at which the agent buys any distractor test, is located to a fraction of that step. The distractor fraction, the share of total sensing usage (all observation actions in an episode) that goes to the distractor test, is exactly $0$ for $w \le 3.5$, is $0.103 \pm 0.001$ at $w{=}4$, reaches $0.233 \pm 0.003$ by $w{=}5$, and saturates in the $0.330$--$0.332$ range for $w \ge 31.6$ (seed-level SE $0.004$--$0.005$, Figure~\ref{fig:distractor}). The onset therefore lies in the bracket $(3.5, 4.0]$.

Ordinary information gain does not distinguish reward-relevant from reward-irrelevant uncertainty, so once the weight makes the distractor's nonzero but task-useless information gain worth its cost, Planning+IG spends budget on it. EFE at the canonical $w{=}1$ stays at zero distractor fraction on this instance only because the onset bracket $(3.5, 4.0]$ lies above $1$, not because EFE is structurally immune. The root cause is that $I(b)$ is computed over the full joint belief rather than over the quantities the pending commit decision depends on. The repair scores information gain on the reward-relevant marginal, $\tilde{I}_a(b) = \mathbb{E}_{o\sim Q(\cdot\mid b,a)} D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big[Q(s_{\mathrm{rel}} \mid b,o,a) \,\|\, Q(s_{\mathrm{rel}} \mid b,a)\big]$, restricted to the state components $s_{\mathrm{rel}}$ the commit reward depends on. This is the ordinary expected information gain $I_a(b)$ of Section~\ref{sec:methodology} evaluated on the belief over $s_{\mathrm{rel}}$ instead of the full joint belief, so the only change is which belief the epistemic term is scored on.

In the implementation, $s_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is the reward-equivalence class of the state. Two states are reward-equivalent when every commit action pays the same in both, so the partition into classes is read directly off the commit reward matrix the agent is given (Section~\ref{sec:methodology}), and information gain is scored on the class marginal. On \texttt{DistractorDiagnosisEnv} the two states that share a condition and differ only in the nuisance bit have the same commit-reward column, so the four classes are exactly the four conditions. The finite-horizon lookahead still propagates the full joint posterior, and on an environment where no two states are reward-equivalent the variant reduces exactly to ordinary information gain.

Sweeping both agents over the same refined grid makes the effect a paired curve (Figure~\ref{fig:distractor}). The relevance-weighted agent takes zero distractor tests at every swept weight, against $6.46$ tests and $33.2\%$ of total usage for ordinary information gain at $w{=}100$, and recovers the reward that ordinary information gain gives up by buying them. Listing ordinary information gain's mean reward first, the pairs are $-2.45$ against $-1.45$ at $w{=}4$, $-4.31$ against $-1.45$ at both $w{=}5$ and $w{=}10$, and $-10.48 \pm 0.11$ against $-3.64 \pm 0.36$ at $w{=}100$ (seed-level SE). Success rates are identical through $w{=}31.6$, and the variant's is nominally higher at $w{=}100$ ($99.2\%$ against $98.4\%$, not significant). Seed-level Welch tests with Holm--Bonferroni correction over the weight-by-metric family (every swept weight and reported metric, corrected together) confirm the usage and distractor-count differences at every weight past onset and the reward difference at $w{=}31.6$ and $w{=}100$ ($p{=}1.2{\times}10^{-5}$ and $1.5{\times}10^{-5}$), but not the smaller reward differences at $w{=}4$, $5$, and $10$.





Information-directed sampling (IDS) \citep{russo2014}, which is explicitly reward-aware through its information-ratio numerator, the squared expected regret of taking the observation action (Appendix~\ref{app:theory_agents}), is not immune either, for an implementation reason. Its denominator, information about the optimal commit (\texttt{info\_\allowbreak astar} in the implementation), is correctly zero for the distractor action, and the ratio is then undefined. The implementation falls back to a raw state-entropy reduction (\texttt{info\_\allowbreak state}) whenever \texttt{info\_\allowbreak astar} is at or near zero, which lets the distractor's nuisance-bit informativeness through. IDS's distractor fraction is $0.305 \pm 0.005$ (seed-level SE), measurably below Planning+IG's saturated $0.330$--$0.332$ (seed-level SE $0.004$--$0.005$, roughly a $3$-SE gap) but well above zero. This is evidence against that implementation pattern, which reintroduces the reward-blindness the reward-aware measure was meant to avoid, not against reward-aware information measures in general. Neither ordinary information gain nor this IDS adaptation is a clean immune baseline against reward-irrelevant sensing on this benchmark.

The relevance-weighted variant has no such fallback. It scores ordinary information gain on a coarsened state space, so a test uninformative about the reward-equivalence classes earns exactly zero. Appendix~\ref{app:ids} reports the IDS baseline in full on the observe-then-commit environments.

\subsection{Distractor Robustness under Reward-Irrelevant Sensing}
\label{app:distractor_details}

Section~\ref{sec:distractor} gives the refined-grid protocol, curves, relevance partition and corrected comparison family. Appendix~\ref{app:distractor} establishes the factorization guarantee. The relevance variant changes only the belief on which information gain is scored,
\[
\tilde I_a(b)=\mathbb E_{o\sim Q(\cdot\mid b,a)}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[Q(s_{\mathrm{rel}}\mid b,o,a)\,\|\,Q(s_{\mathrm{rel}}\mid b,a)\right],
\]
where $s_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is the reward-equivalence class determined by commit payoffs. The lookahead still propagates the full joint posterior.

The remaining reward pairs, ordinary versus relevance-weighted information gain, are $-2.45/-1.45$ at $w=4$ and $-4.31/-1.45$ at both $w=5$ and $10$. These nominal improvements do not survive Holm correction over all weights and reported metrics. At $w=100$, success is $98.4\%/99.2\%$, also not significantly different. Reward differences survive only at $31.6$ and $100$, as reported in the main text.

The IDS adaptation's \texttt{info\_\allowbreak astar} correctly vanishes for the distractor, but its near-zero-denominator fallback to \texttt{info\_\allowbreak state} rewards nuisance information. Its distractor fraction is $0.305\pm0.005$, versus ordinary information gain's saturated $0.330$--$0.332$ (SE $0.004$--$0.005$). The relevance variant has no fallback and buys zero distractor tests. This isolates a flaw in that IDS implementation pattern, not in reward-aware information measures generally. Appendix~\ref{app:ids} reports its broader results.
rationale: Eliminate duplicated main study exposition; retain exact marginal score and remaining nonsignificant findings.
retained_evidence: Factorization scope, known reward-class requirement, formula, non-significant low-weight reward gains, nonsignificant success gap, and IDS fallback limitation retained.

\subsection{Core Environments}
\label{app:core_details}

Table~\ref{tab:main} compares Myopic, same-horizon Planning, EFE, and success-tuned Planning+IG. Appendix~\ref{app:full_tables} adds the remaining baselines and pooled episode-level SE, while the main table uses seed-level SE. Both are in the CSVs and neither is necessarily smaller. The full tables omit untuned Info Gain rows identical to Myopic and Tiger's \texttt{pymdp}-AIF row identical to Posterior-vote (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak tiger.csv}).

Tiger's EFE/Planning identity is measured, not structural. One listen contributes at most one bit, hence one reward unit at the implemented weight, and never changes the reward-based choice at these stakes with shared recursion and tie-breaking. The trajectories match on every metric (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak tiger\_\allowbreak stats.csv}). On Diagnosis and Bandit, EFE Pareto-dominates Planning under Section~\ref{sec:results}'s tests, while success-tuned weights buy greater accuracy at a reward cost.

Epistemic-only commits immediately at chance success on Tiger, Diagnosis, Bandit, and Tileworld-$6{\times}6$ ($49.7\%$, $24.7\%$, $24.7\%$, and $2.9\%$). Removing reward-aware stopping therefore causes non-exploration here (Table~\ref{tab:agents}, Appendix~\ref{app:full_tables}).

Posterior-vote, which draws $100$ states from the belief and takes the majority vote over each sample's optimal action with no information-gain term, is the closest competitor among agents that do not tie EFE exactly. On Bandit it is not significantly different from EFE on any metric (reward $+6.32$ against $+6.27$, seed-level Welch $p{=}0.58$, success $87.0\%$ against $86.9\%$, $p{=}0.97$, inspections $5.01$ against $5.11$, $p{=}0.30$), and on Testbed it ties reward-only Planning exactly and beats EFE. It does not transfer. On Diagnosis it tracks Planning rather than EFE ($-2.78$ against EFE's $-1.37$), and on Tiger it is well behind ($+3.79$ against $+5.19$). Bootstrap 95\% CIs (10{,}000 resamples over 5{,}000 episodes, Appendix~\ref{app:stats}) confirm non-overlapping Bandit reward intervals between EFE ($[6.18, 6.37]$) and Planning ($[5.64, 5.86]$).



Pooled episode-level effect sizes distinguish small reward changes from success gains (Table~\ref{tab:effect_sizes}). EFE versus Planning has reward $d{=}0$ on Tiger and $|d|<0.15$ on Diagnosis and Bandit, with success $d\approx0.33$ and $0.40$ on the latter two. These small success effects accompany the reward Pareto dominance reported above.

Equal episodes per seed make seed-level and pooled mean differences identical, so matching signs provide no independent check. Seed-level tests use five independent replications rather than $5{,}000$ episodes. Diagnosis and Bandit retain Holm significance on reward and success at that level, while Tiger remains an exact tie. We do not interpret seed-level Cohen's $d$: the smaller, noisy standard deviation of five means inflates magnitudes by roughly $6$--$90$ times relative to pooled values in the committed \texttt{*\_\allowbreak stats.csv} files. Inference instead uses seed-level $p$-values and confidence intervals.

The large EFE/Planning reward effect occurs on Tileworld-$8{\times}8$ ($|d|{=}1.13$, \texttt{results\_\allowbreak tileworld\_\allowbreak 8x8\_\allowbreak stats.csv}), where Planning takes no scans at the tested horizon. At $6{\times}6$ both scan and the effect is negligible ($d\approx0.01$). Against success-tuned Info Gain and Planning+IG, the largest reward effect is medium, $d{=}0.69$ on Testbed.

\subsection{RockSample as an Interleaved Observe-Act Setting}
\label{app:rocksample_main_details}

This subsection extends Section~\ref{sec:rocksample} on the cost-modified RockSample variant of \citet{smith2004} specified in Appendix~\ref{app:experimental_protocol}. The agent moves on a grid among rocks of hidden quality, and the actions are the four cardinal moves (N/S/E/W), one check per rock, sample, and exit. Proposition~\ref{prop:factored} covers the check and navigation actions, and Remark~\ref{rem:transition-aware} states its boundary for state-altering sensing.

The agents under comparison fall into two groups. The first is the weighted family, meaning the Planning, Planning+IG, and EFE agents (Table~\ref{tab:rocksample} abbreviates Planning+IG as Plan+IG), which use depth-limited belief-space tree search over factored beliefs (independent per-rock). The search depth is the $d$ in each row label of Table~\ref{tab:rocksample}, depth 3 or 4 on the three smaller instances and depth 2 on RS[11,11]. All three share one hand-coded leaf evaluation (\texttt{rho\_\allowbreak aif/\allowbreak agents/\allowbreak rocksample\_\allowbreak agents.py}) that, at the depth limit, greedily plans the remainder of the episode. That leaf rule scores each rock not yet sampled by its belief-weighted sample value, the belief that the rock is good times the good-sample payoff plus the belief that it is bad times the bad-sample penalty. It considers only the rocks whose value is positive, moves to the one whose value net of the move cost of reaching it is highest and samples it, repeats, and exits when no such rock remains. Because these three agents share that leaf value, they differ only in the information gain weight $w$.

The second group holds the reference agents. POMCP is a search-tree solver, run at a configuration tuned once on separate seeds and then held fixed (Appendix~\ref{app:rocksample}). The row labeled ``Rollout only'' runs POMCP's approach-then-check rule standalone, with no search tree. That rule is POMCP's rollout policy, the default policy that plays out each simulation once it leaves the search tree, and it is a hand-coded, unbounded-horizon rule rather than a depth-limited search. It walks to the unresolved rock with the highest belief per unit of distance (the nearest one at a uniform prior), checks it at close range where accuracy is $0.95$, samples if the belief crosses a threshold, writes off any rock whose belief falls below $0.15$, and exits when nothing is left. The prose below calls this standalone run the heuristic. Greedy, the remaining row, samples without checking.



Across the three smaller instances the reading is the same. EFE at $w{=}1$ is never significantly behind the $w{=}5$ comparator of Table~\ref{tab:rocksample}, is ahead of it once, and is statistically tied with or below the heuristic. On RS[5,3], EFE and Planning+IG ($w{=}5$) are not significantly different ($+16.47$ vs.\ $+16.41$, seed-level Welch $p{=}0.74$, a failure to reject, not a TOST-backed equivalence claim). Both are bolded in Table~\ref{tab:rocksample} as statistical ties with the best row, which is the heuristic at $+16.67$. On RS[7,4], EFE leads the weighted family outright ($+15.96$ vs.\ $+14.56$ for Planning+IG, $p<10^{-5}$) and is statistically tied with the heuristic's $+15.85$ ($p{=}0.65$, again a failure to reject rather than demonstrated equivalence). On RS[7,8], EFE and Planning+IG ($w{=}5$) are again not significantly different from each other ($+21.85$ vs.\ $+23.76$, $p{=}0.09$ uncorrected, not significant after Holm--Bonferroni), while both substantially outperform Planning ($+12.31$, $p<10^{-4}$). On this instance the heuristic reaches $+28.33 \pm 0.82$ on the identical protocol. Both deficits against it survive the per-metric Holm correction (Planning+IG $p{=}2.4{\times}10^{-3}$, EFE $p{=}4.6{\times}10^{-4}$), so the table bolds the heuristic alone there. Planning, Planning+IG, and EFE all sit below that $+28.33$, so on RS[7,8] these are relative comparisons within a family that is jointly suboptimal.

More checking beyond $w{=}5$ never significantly helps on these three instances and twice significantly hurts, with $w{=}10$ falling to $+20.55$ on RS[7,8] ($p{=}0.003$, significant under the per-metric Holm family) and to $+14.60$ on RS[5,3] ($p{=}3.5{\times}10^{-9}$), while the same step is flat on RS[7,4] ($p{=}0.18$), where EFE at $w{=}1$ had already beaten both tuned weights (Appendix~\ref{app:rocksample}). We ran only $w \in \{5, 10\}$ as tuned comparators on RockSample, not the nine-point grid used for the observe-then-commit environments (Section~\ref{sec:methodology}), so on RS[7,8], where $w{=}5$ attains the highest reward of the three weights we ran and is not significantly different from $w{=}1$, this identifies the best of three sampled weights rather than a grid-searched argmax, and we make no claim that $w{=}5$ is the reward-maximizing weight over a denser sweep.

The Bad and Good columns of Table~\ref{tab:rocksample} are the mean numbers of bad and good rocks sampled per episode. On RS[5,3], RS[7,4], and RS[7,8], EFE samples $0.01$ to $0.06$ bad rocks per episode against Greedy's $1.51$ to $3.98$, with seed-level Welch $p<5{\times}10^{-8}$ at every instance.

EFE's gap over $w{=}0$ Planning, largest on RS[7,8] among the three smaller instances, does not extend to RS[11,11] ($|S|{=}2{,}048$), where EFE and Planning achieve identical reward ($+13.23$ each) despite that instance having the most rocks to check. Every tree-search agent vastly outperforms Greedy ($+12.9$ to $+13.2$ against $-18.9$), but nothing here differentiates EFE from reward-only planning. Every tree-search agent at its reported configuration converges to the same conservative pattern of checking one or two nearby rocks, sampling if a rock looks good, and exiting, so the weight on information gain moves reward by at most $0.06$. This includes POMCP at its frozen setting (Appendix~\ref{app:rocksample}). Moving from the table's depth 2 to depth 3 does not change this. Rerunning at depth 3 (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak rocksample\_\allowbreak 11x11\_\allowbreak depth3\_\allowbreak check.csv}) costs seconds and reproduces the same pattern within 1 SE, with Planning and EFE at $+13.23$ and Planning+IG at $+13.17$.

Two explanations fit that collapse, either no exploitable slack or slack that no depth-limited search can reach, and the heuristic in Table~\ref{tab:rocksample} settles which holds. Bound by no search depth, and walking up to a rock before spending a check on it, it scores $+28.66 \pm 0.83$ on RS[11,11] on the table's $5$ seeds and $100$ episodes, where every tree-search agent, EFE and POMCP included, sits in the $+12.94$ to $+13.23$ band, and $+28.33 \pm 0.82$ on RS[7,8] against the best tree-search agent's $+23.76 \pm 0.58$. There is therefore a great deal of slack at 11 widely spaced rocks that the depth-limited belief-space search cannot reach. The Good column shows it in behavioral terms, since on RS[11,11] the heuristic samples $5.22$ good rocks per episode while every tree-search agent samples about half a rock.

The mechanism is now identifiable. Recall that check accuracy decays with the agent's distance from the rock (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}), so a check is informative only when taken from close range. Reaching close range means walking to the rock first. At this instance the checks that could be informative are far from the agent, and a depth-2 or depth-3 tree cannot represent the walk that would make them informative. Within its horizon only a single check taken from the agent's own starting cell is worth making, so the weight on information gain has almost nothing to act on. The shared greedy leaf rule values a rock at its belief-weighted sample reward, which is exactly zero at the uniform prior because at belief $0.5$ the $+10$ good-sample payoff and the $-10$ bad-sample penalty cancel. So no rock passes the rule's positive-value filter, and it recommends the exit. Because the informative checks lie beyond the depths we run, depth 3 leaves reward unchanged and every weight gives the same reward to within $0.06$, with the higher weights buying only about half an extra check per episode.

One further detail of that leaf deserves disclosure. Its completion estimate charges move costs for a walk to the east edge before collecting the exit reward (\texttt{rocksample\_\allowbreak agents.py}), while the environment pays the exit from any cell. This phantom travel cost deflates every depth-capped continuation relative to the exact value of exiting immediately, a bias toward earlier exits. The immediate exit escapes the deflation because an exit taken inside the tree at the current cell is valued at its true payoff, so only continuations that run on to the leaf carry the charge. Every agent in the family uses this same leaf rule, so the reported comparisons are conditional on it. But it means the leaf's exit recommendation is overdetermined here rather than resting on the zero prior expectation alone.

POMCP corroborates the mechanism from the other side. A deeper POMCP tree gains the lookahead to plan a walk out to the distant rocks, but, on our reading of its behavioral trace (Appendix~\ref{app:rocksample}), its in-tree checks are still taken from a distance where accuracy is low, and its reward falls monotonically from $+12.94$ at $H{=}10$ to $-54.78$ at $H{=}40$. Reach alone, without walking up before checking, is not enough.

This is a limitation of the tree-search family at feasible depths on this instance, not evidence about information-gain weighting, and it bounds what RockSample[11,11] can be asked to show about EFE. Per-instance detail, including the standalone heuristic on every instance, is in Appendix~\ref{app:rocksample}.

The RS[11,11] collapse, the RS[7,8] advantage, and the Tileworld scaling result read as one mechanism seen at three points. EFE's advantage over reward-only Planning tracks how much slack a problem's structure leaves between the reward-only policy's default behavior and the information-optimal behavior that the agent's search can actually represent, not problem size or observation-action count in themselves. On Tileworld, reward-only Planning scans too little to disambiguate a large grid, so directed information gain buys a large success-rate margin. On RS[7,8], eight rocks spread across a mid-sized grid leave real ambiguity about which are worth sampling. On RS[11,11] no check beyond the agent's own cell is worth taking within the depths we run, so the weight has almost nothing to act on. We did not design instances to stress-test this reading, so it remains a mechanistic interpretation of the four RockSample instances and three Tileworld scales already reported rather than an independently validated scaling law.

\subsection{The Information-Unit Weight and Tuning}
EFE fixes the exploration--exploitation weight at $w{=}1$ rather than eliminating it (Section~\ref{subsec:formal_rho_equiv}), and $w{=}1$ is tuned to neither criterion, unlike the reward-maximizing weight $w^*_{\text{ret}}$ or the success-maximizing weight $w^*_{\text{succ}}$ ($10$ to $50$) used for Planning+IG in the main tables. That its measured reward sits inside the reward-maximizing tied run on three of the five swept environments is an empirical finding of the Pareto sweep (Section~\ref{sec:pareto}, Appendix~\ref{app:pareto_details}), not a design target. Applications that require near-certain accuracy may warrant a higher weight, which must still be tuned per environment, so EFE provides a principled starting point rather than a scale-free automatic calibration. The weight's dependence on the reward scale and on the bit-versus-nat convention is set out in the reward-to-nats calibration discussion in Appendix~\ref{app:theory_setup}.

A further complication for tuning is that adding planning depth to a weighted IG bonus amplifies the weight's effect, so the tuning problem becomes harder with depth. The same weight buys more sensing at depth two than at depth one, so the map from weight to sensing usage shifts with the horizon. A weight tuned at one depth need not carry over to another. One measurement supports this directly. At $w{=}100$ on Bandit under the canonical 5-seed protocol, Planning+IG at $H{=}2$ takes $12.36$ inspections against myopic Info Gain's $11.50$ (seed-level Welch $p{=}0.003$, \url{experiments/run_bandit_w100_depth_comparison.py}).

The requirement for a sufficient planning horizon also has a discount-factor form. In the discount sweep (Appendix~\ref{app:discount}, Table~\ref{tab:discount}), EFE's success advantage over Planning on Diagnosis and Bandit is significant at $\gamma \in \{0.99, 1.0\}$ and not at $\gamma \in \{0.90, 0.95\}$, because heavier discounting truncates the effective planning horizon below the number of observations needed for disambiguation. The sweep covers four discount factors on three environments, so it does not establish a general threshold, but it does show that applications whose time pressure mandates discounting as heavy as $\gamma{=}0.95$ on Diagnosis-like problems should not expect EFE's epistemic drive to pay off.

\subsection{Approximate Planning with MCTS-EFE}
At each depth the tree branches over $K$ observation actions and then, per action, over its $|\mathcal{O}|$ observation outcomes, so the exact tree search cost is $\mathcal{O}((K \cdot |\mathcal{O}|)^H)$, limiting practical horizons to $H{=}2$--$3$ with $K \geq 3$. To push beyond this, we implement MCTS-EFE, a UCB1 tree search whose design choices we state in turn. The tree branches over observe and commit actions and, after each observe action, enumerates its $|\mathcal{O}|$ observation outcomes as child nodes. It adds the exact per-node information gain to the in-tree reward of each observe action, so that within the tree an observation is credited for what it reveals as well as charged for what it costs. Values propagate by max-backup, each node taking the maximum over its children's values rather than the average of the returns sampled through it. Leaves are scored by an EFE-greedy rollout, which at each step takes the observation with the best one-step EFE value and credits the better of committing now and continuing to observe. The UCB1 exploration constant is left at its default, the commit reward range (110 on Tiger). That default is a static analog of the $R_{\mathrm{hi}} - R_{\mathrm{lo}}$ rule of \citet{silver2010}, which sizes the constant to the spread between the highest and lowest returns seen in preliminary sample runs of the search, whereas the default here takes the spread once from the commit reward table and never revisits it. On Tiger at $H{=}10$, MCTS-EFE with 500 simulations achieves $97.7\% \pm 0.5$pp success ($14$--$16$ ms per episode across the three horizons tested, \texttt{results\_\allowbreak mcts\_\allowbreak efe.csv}), compared to $88.1\% \pm 0.2$pp for POMCP at the same simulation count ($11$--$12$ ms per episode across horizons, seed-level SE, seed-level Welch $p{=}4.4{\times}10^{-6}$). The comparison is simulation-matched, not compute-matched, since MCTS-EFE's leaf evaluations are more expensive per simulation. In this configuration, EFE's closed-form information valuation, acting as the in-tree observe reward and inside the leaf rollouts, outperforms POMCP's semi-informed rollouts (Appendix~\ref{app:pomcp}).

An ablation of the two components that distinguish this search from a UCT tree, the in-tree information gain and the max-backup (Table~\ref{tab:mcts-ablation}, Appendix~\ref{app:pomcp}), finds neither detectably load-bearing at five seeds after Holm correction. What remains to carry the contribution is the EFE-greedy leaf rollout together with the exact belief representation and the exact commit-child values, which the ablation holds fixed. A commit child is the node reached by a commit action, and the search sets its value to the belief-expected commit reward computed directly from the belief instead of estimating it from sampled returns.

Appendix~\ref{app:pomcp} addresses the two natural objections, that the POMCP gap reflects an untuned exploration constant or POMCP's rollout policy (Table~\ref{tab:pomcp-sweep}). Tuning the constant narrows the Tiger gap without removing it. With both solvers' constants selected on tuning seeds disjoint from every evaluation seed, under a rule recorded before the runs reported there and written after an exploratory sweep on the canonical seeds had been inspected, MCTS-EFE stays significantly ahead on Tiger success and reward. Where the agent must choose among tests, neither the constant nor information-gain rollouts removes more than a small part of the gap, which stays above twenty-five points on Diagnosis and above eighty points on Tileworld-$6{\times}6$ at every swept configuration. Because the EFE-greedy leaf evaluation, exact beliefs, and exact commit-child values were held fixed together in the sweep, the rollout check, and the ablation, we attribute the gap to that joint configuration and not to directed observation selection in isolation. Separating them would need a further matched-compute comparison that we have not run. The claim is not that EFE-based planning exceeds state-of-the-art POMDP solvers, but that the EFE objective supplies a principled, zero-tuning in-tree reward and leaf evaluation in place of hand-designed rollouts.

The approach also scales to multiple observation actions. For single-observation environments such as Tiger, the observation-outcome enumeration (2 outcomes per action) keeps expansion costs low, and the question is whether the same holds once the agent must choose among several tests. On Diagnosis ($N{=}4$, $K{=}2$ tests), MCTS-EFE at $H{=}5$ achieves $94.2\% \pm 0.5$pp success compared to POMCP's $65.5\% \pm 2.1$pp at the same simulation count (200 simulations, seed-level SE, seed-level Welch $p{=}1.1{\times}10^{-4}$, \texttt{results\_\allowbreak mcts\_\allowbreak efe.csv}). To exercise the approach on a larger multi-observation environment, we evaluate on Tileworld $6{\times}6$ ($|S|{=}36$, $K{=}6$ scans). MCTS-EFE saturates at $95.4\% \pm 0.6$pp success across both simulation budgets tested (200 and 500, seed-level SE), well above the $71.9\% \pm 1.5$pp of Exact-EFE (the full recursive EFE agent, called EFE in the earlier tables, evaluated here within the same MCTS battery), but at a reward cost ($-25.02$ vs.\ Exact-EFE's $-21.62$) from scanning substantially more (32.3 vs.\ 14.8 observations on average). MCTS's sampled rollouts do not value information as precisely as the exact recursion, so it trades reward for a large success-rate gain by scanning more thoroughly. On Tiger and Diagnosis there is no such trade, since MCTS-EFE sits slightly below Exact-EFE on success and further below it on reward ($97.7\%$ against $99.9\%$ and $+3.73$ against $+5.65$ on Tiger, $94.2\%$ against $97.1\%$ and $-3.26$ against $-1.44$ on Diagnosis). POMCP collapses on this larger observation menu regardless of simulation budget ($2.6\% \pm 0.4$pp at 200 simulations, $3.9\% \pm 0.5$pp at 500, seed-level SE, with $0.09$ scans per episode). MCTS-EFE's $91$--$93$pp success-rate gap over POMCP (seed-level Welch $p<10^{-9}$ at both budgets) therefore shows that the gap persists at this scale, even though the specific reward/success trade-off MCTS-EFE strikes here differs from the smaller environments. With almost no scans, POMCP commits on a nearly uninformed belief, and its success sits near the $1/36$ rate of an uninformed guess. For larger observation spaces, more efficient tree policies, such as progressive widening or double progressive widening \citep{sunberg2018,benchetrit2025}, techniques that limit how many children a node expands as a function of its visit count, would further improve scalability. We leave this to future work.

\subsection{Approximate Planning with MCTS-EFE}

Exact enumeration costs $\mathcal O((K|\mathcal O|)^H)$ for $K$ sensing actions with $|\mathcal O|$ outcomes each. MCTS-EFE uses UCB1 over observe/commit actions, enumerates each observation action's outcomes, adds exact per-node information gain, and backs up maxima. EFE-greedy leaf rollouts compare immediate commitment with the best one-step EFE observation. Commit-child values are exact belief-expected rewards. The default exploration constant is the fixed commit-reward range, $110$ on Tiger, rather than the preliminary-return range used by \citet{silver2010}. Appendix~\ref{app:pomcp} reports exploration tuning, informed rollouts, the ablation and a separate compute-matched Tiger control.

The simulation-matched comparison uses $500$ simulations on Tiger at $H=10$. MCTS-EFE reaches $97.7\%\pm0.5$ percentage points against POMCP's $88.1\%\pm0.2$ ($p=4.4\times10^{-6}$). Its cost is $14$--$16$ ms per episode across tested horizons, versus $11$--$12$ ms for POMCP, so matching simulations does not match computation. At $H=5$ and $200$ simulations on Diagnosis, the corresponding success rates are $94.2\%\pm0.5$ and $65.5\%\pm2.1$ ($p=1.1\times10^{-4}$). These are seed-level SEs and Welch tests from \texttt{results\_\allowbreak mcts\_\allowbreak efe.csv}.

On Tileworld-$6\times6$, MCTS-EFE reaches $95.4\%\pm0.6$ at both $200$ and $500$ simulations, compared with Exact-EFE's $71.9\%\pm1.5$ under this battery's protocol. The gain costs reward ($-25.02/-21.62$) and observations ($32.3/14.8$). POMCP reaches only $2.6\%\pm0.4$ and $3.9\%\pm0.5$, with about $0.09$ scans per episode. The success gaps have $p<10^{-9}$ at both budgets. On Tiger and Diagnosis, MCTS-EFE instead falls below Exact-EFE on both success ($97.7/99.9\%$, $94.2/97.1\%$) and reward ($3.73/5.65$, $-3.26/-1.44$). Thus approximate search does not uniformly improve either metric.

The controls detect no success or reward effect of either switchable component, in-tree information gain and max-backup, after Holm correction at five seeds. EFE leaf evaluation, exact beliefs and exact commit-child values remain coupled. The exploration selection uses disjoint tuning seeds but its rule was written after inspecting the canonical-seed sweep, so Tiger's tuned comparison is retrospective. These results concern the joint implementation, not isolated directed sensing or general superiority over POMDP solvers. Progressive widening methods \citep{sunberg2018,benchetrit2025} are possible extensions for larger observation spaces, not evaluated improvements here.
rationale: Keep method and nonduplicated per-environment results, cite the early POMCP appendix for its complete controls rather than repeat every tuning result.
